title: Did Zhuge Liang's Wooden Ox Walk by Itself? What Records of the Three Kingdoms Says
description:
Did the wooden ox and gliding horse really haul grain for Zhuge Liang?
For viewers who want to know how the histories record the wooden ox and gliding horse (muniu liuma), and which parts of their design are still uncertain.

Records of the Three Kingdoms records wooden oxen hauling grain in 231, the making of gliding horses and wooden oxen finished in 232, and gliding horses hauling grain in 234; even so, the army still set up farming garrisons to keep its food coming. Pei Songzhi's annotations quote the Collected Works of Zhuge Liang, preserving "one leg, four feet," axle holes, square sacks and measurements, but these words alone cannot settle whether it had walking legs or how many wheels it had. The copying and the tongue mechanism in chapter 102 of the later Romance of the Three Kingdoms are scenes from the novel.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated story aids, not definitive mechanical reconstructions. Fixed editions of the sources and a line-by-line comparison are listed below. Information checked as of 2026-10-19.

chapters.wood-001: The grain train leaves the valley, still under cloth

ox001.text: Spring 234: Zhuge Liang's army marches out of the Xie Valley; grain heads to the front.

ox002.text: Hauling devices go up the valley too. What were they called?

ox003.text: We keep them under cloth here; their true form is still unknown.

ox004.text: An old book's notes lie open, crowded with part names; can they show us what's under the cloth?

ox005.text: Could these devices keep a whole army fed?

ox006.text: Three years earlier at Qishan, grain moved too. What were those devices called?

ox007.text: A later surviving text adds a phrase: "one leg, four feet." Could it really walk?

ox008.text: A much later novel has someone twist its "tongue." What happens next?

ox009.text: Which scenes come from old records, and which from later stories?

ox010.text: Spring 231: grain moves along Qishan's mountain roads with the army.

ox011.text: Zhuge Liang sets out again to besiege Qishan.

ox012.text: Liu Shan's biography says only: "First hauled by wooden ox."

ox013.text: The Qishan device was the wooden ox; "first" marks this as when it hauled grain.

ox014.text: No word on how many were built or what each carried.

ox015.text: The oxen made the war record; can the supply line last to the sixth month?

ox016.text: The front must feed not one person but a whole army.

ox017.text: In the sixth month that summer, grain ran out and the army withdrew.

ox018.text: He withdrew. The oxen didn't erase that shortage from history.

ox019.text: Does that prove the wooden ox was useless? No.

ox021.text: One campaign, oxen in use, grain short: which number is missing?

ox022.text: With no count and no distance, we can't work out their total capacity.

ox024.text: If oxen hauled at Qishan, why does Huangsha, a year later, say horses and oxen were finished?

ox025.text: At Qishan, "haul" means on the road; at Huangsha, "finished" means built: two different steps.

ox026.text: It reads: "Gliding horses and wooden oxen done; troops drilled."

ox027.text: That year at Huangsha, Zhuge Liang rested his troops, and urged farming: beyond devices, he needed grain.

ox028.text: Was this improving old devices, adding new ones, or finishing a batch?

ox030.text: No counts, no steps, nor whether the horse and ox were the same size.

ox034.text: The ox has a date of use. When is the gliding horse first said to haul grain?

ox035.text: Two years on, a campaign record finally pairs the gliding horse with "haul."

ox037.text: It reads: "First hauled by gliding horse."

ox039.text: That doesn't mean the first one was built that month.

ox040.text: His biography: the army reaches Wuzhang Plains.

ox041.text: We're at Wuzhang Plains now. Can grain from afar keep up?

ox042.text: Zhuge Liang "always worried that grain would not keep up."

ox043.text: So he split off troops to farm, preparing to stay long.

ox100.text: Soldier-farmers lived among Wei River locals, the fields near the front.

ox108.text: The armies faced off for over a hundred days; that length was the problem hauling and farming both faced.

ox101.text: Holding the line and farming, the front grew part of its own food.

ox044.text: Gliding horses and farming, side by side: which truly carried the army?

ox045.text: How much did the horses haul? No total given.

ox046.text: And how much did farming add? No harvest table here either.

ox047.text: So the shortage proves neither that they failed nor that they solved it all.

ox049.text: This isn't a magic machine suddenly breaking; supply was tight all along.

ox050.text: Yet if the history names the hauling tools, could their shape be on another page?

ox051.text: Zhuge Liang's biography praises his ingenuity, naming both devices.

ox052.text: Chen Shou writes: "Ox and horse were both his ideas."

ox053.text: It credits the idea to Zhuge Liang but never draws them.

ox054.text: Details come only in Pei Songzhi's annotations.

ox055.text: Pei quotes the Collected Works of Zhuge Liang: "How to make them."

ox056.text: A commentator quoting a text; it doesn't mean Pei measured the devices.

ox057.text: That opening "one leg, four feet" is in the ox passage, after "square belly, curved head."

ox058.text: Those words suggest a shape with a belly and a head.

ox059.text: But which part is a "foot"? How does it attach?

ox060.text: The text also names "twin shafts," another part.

ox102.text: The ox passage also says "the tongue attaches to the belly": another part.

ox103.text: It puts the tongue on the belly; it never says a twist stops it.

ox061.text: "One leg, four feet" doesn't say any part flexes; that alone can't prove it walked.

ox062.text: The text even says: "Man walks six chi, ox walks four steps."

ox063.text: Man and ox side by side: did the device really walk by itself?

ox064.text: But "walks" states the motion's effect, not how each joint moves.

ox065.text: Pei's quote adds "and men don't tire much," yet not how many escort it.

ox066.text: It says the ox "carries a year's grain." Can that convert to today's weight?

ox104.text: It also separates "alone, dozens of li; in a group, twenty li."

ox105.text: Two modes, recorded apart, with no word on what road.

ox067.text: It's an old hauling description, not a capacity test we could replicate.

ox068.text: No. It never says how many people's grain, so kilos have no solid base.

ox069.text: Nor can these distances give total supply apart from roads, crews and numbers.

ox070.text: Then the text switches headings: "Dimensions of the gliding horse."

ox071.text: It lists ribs, front and rear axle holes, front and rear poles; what fits those holes?

ox072.text: Like a carpenter's parts list, not a finished build.

ox073.text: Holes are named axle, leg and pole holes; at least we see which parts they serve.

ox075.text: The ox has "one leg, four feet," the horse "four legs, front and rear." Are they the same legs?

ox076.text: We can't tell. The ox and horse are described apart, with no word on whether both "legs" match.

ox077.text: Pei's horse text also lists two square sacks, each 2 hu 3 dou.

ox078.text: Sacks show where the grain went; how did the push reach the frame?

ox079.text: To build the horse from this text, where would the first joint go?

ox081.text: The novel's twist-to-stop trick: in which layer of text does it appear?

ox082.text: In the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, ch. 102, they roam hills as if alive.

ox083.text: In the story, Sima Yi has captured ones taken apart and copied to size.

ox109.text: The novel makes it an arms race: within half a month, Wei copies 2,000-plus to haul grain in Longxi.

ox084.text: Shu troops dressed as Wei join a Wei grain train and lead them off.

ox085.text: Shu soldiers twist the tongue in its mouth and it stops. Can Wei drag it away?

ox106.text: Wei catches up but can't pull or lift them: the novel's trap is sprung.

ox086.text: Tongues twisted back, they move again: a reversal right before Wei.

ox107.text: Shu soldiers pose as spirit troops amid smoke and fire; Wei fears ghosts.

ox087.text: That's the novel. Records of the Three Kingdoms notes their use, not this snatch trick.

ox089.text: If someone shows a reconstruction "fully based on the ancient text," what to ask first?

ox090.text: Point at one joint and find which ancient line it comes from.

ox092.text: The horse's front axle hole sits four cun from the head.

ox094.text: That first joint: names and spacings are given, but not the full order of joining.

ox095.text: If a model can haul grain, it proves only its design works, not that it's the original.

ox098.text: Which part of that text would you most want drawn?
